When a marriage comes to an end, understanding your legal rights and responsibilities is essential. Divorce can feel overwhelming, especially when emotions, finances, and family dynamics are involved. Fortunately, Colorado divorce laws are designed to provide a clear legal framework that helps couples move forward in a fair and structured way.

If you are considering divorce or have already decided to file, having a basic understanding of Colorado divorce laws can help you feel more prepared and confident about the process ahead.

Let’s break it down step by step.

Understanding Divorce Laws in Colorado

Colorado is considered a no-fault divorce state, meaning that neither spouse is required to prove wrongdoing, such as infidelity or abuse, in order to file for divorce. Instead, the only requirement in Colorado to obtain a divorce is a determination that the marriage is irretrievably broken.

The legal term “ broken” simply means that the relationship has broken down to the point where reconciliation is not realistic.

This approach is intended to reduce conflict and allow couples to focus on resolving practical matters such as property division, child custody, and financial support.

Residency Requirements for Divorce in Colorado

Before filing for divorce in Colorado, at least one spouse must meet the state’s residency requirement.

To file for divorce:

  • Either you or your spouse must have lived in Colorado for at least 90 days before filing the petition.
  • The residency requirement applies regardless of where the marriage took place.

Failing to meet this requirement can delay your case, so it is important to confirm eligibility before starting the process.

The Waiting Period: What to Expect

Colorado law requires a mandatory waiting period before a divorce can be finalized.

  • There is a 91-day waiting period that begins once the divorce petition is filed and served on the other spouse (or jointly filed).
  • This waiting period applies to all divorces, even if both spouses agree on every issue.

The purpose of this waiting period is to allow time for reflection, negotiation, and resolution of outstanding matters. Even in uncontested divorces, the court cannot issue a final decree until this timeframe has passed.

Key Legal Issues Addressed in a Colorado Divorce

While the divorce laws establish the framework, each case is unique. During a divorce, Colorado courts may address several important legal issues, including:

  • Division of marital property and debts, using the state’s equitable distribution standard.
  • Child custody, legally referred to as the parental responsibilities, decision-making and parenting time.
  • Child support, calculated using statutory guidelines.
  • Spousal maintenance (alimony), when appropriate based on the circumstances of the marriage.

Each of these areas follows specific legal standards, and understanding how Colorado law approaches them can help you make informed decisions throughout your case.

Do You Need to Prove Fault in a Colorado Divorce?

No. Colorado’s no-fault system means the court does not consider marital misconduct when deciding whether to grant a divorce.

However, certain behaviors may still be relevant when resolving related issues. For example:

  • Domestic violence can impact custody and parenting time decisions.
  • Financial misconduct may affect how property or debts are divided.

While fault does not determine whether a divorce is granted, it can still play a role in how certain matters are resolved.

Why Understanding Colorado Divorce Laws Matters

Knowing the basics of Colorado divorce laws helps you:

  • Set realistic expectations about timelines and outcomes.
  • Avoid unnecessary delays or procedural mistakes.
  • Better understand your rights and obligations during the process.

Divorce is not just a legal event—it is a major life transition. Being informed allows you to approach it with clarity and confidence.
